meta.title: Pharmy Case Study: One Searchable Clinical Trial Platform | Viesigners
meta.description: How Charles-Erick BG led the UX of one searchable clinical trial platform and tested a two-step form on real traffic.

sections.h1: Turning scattered trial microsites into *one searchable platform*
sections.alt: Clinical trial search interface with results listed beside a map

sections.caption: The hub: search by condition and location, with results on a map. Visuals refreshed by me in 2025.
sections.lead: I led the UX and CRO on this project with the O2Web team. We brought each study’s microsite into one platform, like Airbnb for clinical trials, built around what focus groups said people needed to trust the process.

items.t: A large global pharmaceutical company. Pharmy is a fictional name; the real one is under NDA.
Get more qualification forms from potential trial participants.
UX and CRO expert, leading the UX and CRO.
I worked mainly with a consultant hired by the client. He approved the work, and the client made the final decisions.
A/B test methodology, measurement plan, UX and wireframes for the platform and the form. A graphic designer created the final UI, which stayed very close to my wireframes.

sections.label: The problem
sections.h2: Two problems kept people *from joining a trial*
prose: **People needed to trust the process before searching for a trial.** The client’s focus groups started this project. They showed that people were missing the information they needed to trust the platform and the process, and to decide to join. Distance mattered too: people had to go on site, so they needed a clinic close enough to reach. Yet each study had its own microsite, so the same general information was repeated on each one and harder to maintain.
**The qualification form felt very long.** My audit of the form showed the second problem: people didn’t fill it in and left, and the client relied only on those who finished it.

steps.p: Group the microsites in one searchable platform, like Airbnb for clinical trials, with the general information people needed in one place. That would also make updates easier for the client’s team.

steps.h: Test the form on real traffic
steps.p: My audit of the qualification form led me to suggest a two-step version, which we compared with the one-step form on the same design.

sections.label: Approach
prose: I worked closely with the client’s team to define target user profiles and the indicators that mattered, then wrote the A/B test methodology and measurement plan. I also made sure the measuring tools were in place.
I guided the project team through inspiration, ideation, prototyping and technical validation. The focus groups were run by the client before the project; I built on their findings.

items.h: Split a long form in two steps to capture leads sooner
items.p: The first step collected contact details, so the client could call people, answer their questions and suggest trials by phone, even if they never finished the form.

notes.v: Keep one step, which could have reduced friction a little.
My audit pointed to a long form. I suggested two steps so the client could get leads sooner and wouldn’t rely only on people filling in the whole form.
More build work, such as the UI to go back a step, and a lower finish rate: 28% instead of 35%.

items.h: Give people who don’t qualify a reason to stay
items.p: People who didn’t qualify could join a community through the newsletter.

notes.v: The newsletter kept them in the loop, so the client could reach them again and convert them later.
No downside noted for the client.

items.h: Answer objections before asking people to search
items.p: The homepage explains the project first, and a button then leads to the search.

notes.v: If people have objections, they won’t act. The focus groups showed what was missing, so the right information had to come first.
Everyone lands on an informational page before searching. To limit that, the search stayed the most prominent item in the main menu.

shots.label: How it works or Conditions page

items.h: Make distance visible with a map
items.p: People search by condition and location, and see the trials on a map.

notes.v: The focus groups showed people needed to be close to the clinic because they had to go on site. How far they would travel depended on the disease.
It was much harder to design and build: clusters when zooming out, whether a click zooms or lists the trials, and a list that stays clear on mobile.

items.h: Fit two navigation systems into one platform
items.p: Each microsite had its own navigation, and so did the search platform. The menu had to stay appealing, uncluttered and intuitive, even with both.

notes.v: Stack the two menus and hide them on scroll, or swap to the microsite menu with a clear back button to the platform.
[À FOURNIR : which option shipped, and why?]
Stacked menus are harder to manage on mobile and add cognitive load. Swapping menus is more mobile-first, but needs an intuitive way back.

sections.label: What real users did
sections.h2: What the A/B test *showed, and what it didn’t*

results.t: more leads captured by the two-step form, counting first-step submissions: 5.6% to 8.3% of visits. [À FOURNIR : confirm in your final report, see the note in Claude’s reply]
completion rate per visit, 1.95% to 2.34%. Small sample, not statistically significant.
of version B completions were prequalified candidates. The others joined the community.

reads.p: The two-step form captured more leads, a borderline significant result on this sample. It also separated prequalified candidates from people who joined the community.

On this small sample, the +20% completion rate isn’t statistically significant. I flagged the sample size at the time, and the project moved forward. A smaller share of people finished after the first step, which is the next thing I’d study.
Both versions used the same design, and only the form changed, so the test isolates the form. The numbers come from Google Analytics. I used Hotjar to plan the next iterations in my final report.
The client’s focus groups shaped the project before design started. The design itself wasn’t tested in moderated sessions.

sections.label: Outcome
prose: The platform went live, and the A/B test ran on real traffic. It was a test for the client, and I don’t know whether they kept it.
Today I’d push for a longer test. It wasn’t possible at the time, but it would have given us enough visits to confirm the completion result.
